bibliographic.title: Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance
bibliographic.citation_apa: Hadfield, G. K., & Clark, J. (2026). Regulatory markets: The future of AI governance. Jurimetrics Journal, 65, 195–240.

methodology.method_family: legal and policy analysis; normative institutional design proposal
methodology.study_design: conceptual policy proposal with literature-based argumentation
methodology.technology_context: artificial intelligence broadly, including large generative models, large language models, ChatGPT, generative AI, and dual-use foundation models

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article is a theoretical policy proposal on macro-level AI governance via regulatory markets, with strong relevance to regulation, accountability, and generative AI/LLM context, but the provided text does not center conversational systems, chatbots, agents, or operational conversational governance mechanisms such as guardrails, observability, or human handoff in dialogue.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only partial full text was supplied; keyword screening over-weighted generic governance and LLM mentions relative to conversational governance scope.

appraisal.notes: Appropriate as a high-level institutional governance argument rather than an empirical or conversational-systems study; sampling and ethics appraisal items are largely not applicable.

cerqual.explanation: The proposal is internally coherent and clearly stated, but the supplied evidence supports institutional AI regulation more than conversational LLM governance in regulated deployments.

coding.theme: Macro-level institutional design for AI governance
coding.subtheme: Regulatory markets as an alternative to command-and-control and excessive industry delegation
rq_alignment: accountability and oversight at policy level

synthesis.main_claim: Governments should use regulatory markets—requiring regulated entities to purchase services from government-licensed private regulators—to overcome both the technical deficit of translating law into technical requirements and the democratic deficit of overreliance on industry standards in AI governance.
synthesis.contribution: Offers an institutional policy framework for AI regulation that aims to combine democratically accountable public priorities with market-driven technical regulatory innovation.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual evidence on institutional and policy-level AI governance in regulated settings; not as central evidence on conversational LLM governance, operational controls, or deployment monitoring.

evidence.claim: Peer-reviewed journal article with 2026 Jurimetrics citation
evidence.excerpt: CITATION: Gillian K. Hadfield & Jack Clark, Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance, 65 JURIMETRICS J. 195–240 (2026).

evidence.claim: Authors are Gillian K. Hadfield and Jack Clark
evidence.excerpt: REGULATORY MARKETS: THE FUTURE OF AI GOVERNANCE Gillian K. Hadfield∗ Jack Clark∗∗

evidence.claim: Study is a theoretical policy proposal, not empirical
evidence.excerpt: We propose a solution: regulatory markets, in which governments require the targets of regulation to purchase regulatory services from a government-licensed private regulator.

evidence.claim: Identifies technical and democratic deficits in AI regulation
evidence.excerpt: First is a technical deficit: Legislatures and regulators face significant challenges in rapidly translating conventional command-and-control legal requirements into technical requirements.

evidence.claim: Discusses democratic accountability concern in AI governance
evidence.excerpt: Second is a democratic deficit: Overreliance on industry to provide technical standards fails to ensure that the many values-based decisions that must be made to shape AI development and deployment are made by democratically accountable public, not private, actors.

evidence.claim: Mentions ChatGPT and large generative models
evidence.excerpt: Coming into public view with the release of ChatGPT in November 2022, large generative models, with billions or even trillions of parameters and trained on billions of words and images have shown surprising foundational capacities

evidence.claim: Frames AI governance conversation evolution including ethics and legislation
evidence.excerpt: The past decade has also witnessed an evolution in the conversation around AI governance.

evidence.claim: Links LLM deployment unpredictability to governance challenge
evidence.excerpt: The engineers who develop a facial recognition or large language model cannot possibly anticipate and test for all the different ways in which the models could be used.

evidence.claim: ChatGPT increased regulatory urgency around large language models
evidence.excerpt: Then the dramatic introduction of ChatGPT in late 2022, exposing millions around the world to the potential, and risks, of powerful large language models, increased the sense of urgency around regulation.

evidence.claim: Discusses generative AI and foundation model risk-management policy
evidence.excerpt: The executive order called for NIST to expand its risk-management framework to address generative AI and dual-use foundation models

evidence.claim: No conversational-system governance focus in supplied text
evidence.excerpt: The past decade has also witnessed an evolution in the conversation around AI governance.

evidence.claim: Complex LLMs are difficult to interpret and modify
evidence.excerpt: increasingly, machine-learning models are complex and difficult to interpret and intervention to modify their behavior can be very difficult.
